questions: Are these facial movements involuntary and difficult to suppress?
Do you experience an uncomfortable urge or tension before making the movements that is relieved afterward?
Do the movements disappear during sleep?
Have you been taking antipsychotic, anti-nausea, or antidepressant medication regularly for several months or longer?
Do you also have involuntary movements of your tongue, jaw, or limbs?
Do the involuntary facial contractions affect both sides of your face equally?
Do they mainly consist of forceful, involuntary squeezing of both eyelids shut?
Can you temporarily reduce the contractions by touching your face, wearing tinted glasses, or performing another “sensory trick”?
Are the contractions worse with bright light, stress, fatigue, or speaking?
Did these symptoms begin gradually, rather than suddenly?
Do the contractions predominantly involve one side of your face, beginning around one eye and spreading downward?
During an episode, do you remain fully conscious and able to respond normally?
Do individual episodes last seconds to minutes and recur in attacks?
Do the movements occur only while you are awake?
Have you had any sudden weakness, numbness, loss of speech, or loss of coordination with these episodes?
After an episode, are you confused, unusually sleepy, or unable to remember what happened?
Have you ever bitten your tongue or lost bladder control during an episode?
Do the episodes begin with a sudden abnormal sensation, fear, déjà vu, unusual smell, or rising feeling in the stomach?
Do the facial movements occur in brief, stereotyped episodes that are very similar each time?
Have the episodes ever been recorded while you are asleep?
orders: Video-EEG monitoring with simultaneous facial-muscle EMG to determine whether the episodes are epileptic seizures.
Brain MRI with epilepsy protocol, including thin-cut imaging through the temporal lobes and brainstem.
Neurologic examination during an observed episode, documenting awareness, eye deviation, limb involvement, and response to commands.
Prolonged video-EEG with simultaneous **surface EMG electrodes over the bilateral orbicularis oculi, corrugator, nasalis, and orbicularis oris muscles**, capturing several typical episodes.
Bedside examination for **distractibility, variability, entrainment, and suggestibility** of the facial movements during a typical episode.
Serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, glucose, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and ceruloplasmin.

Overnight video-polysomnography with extended 10–20 EEG and simultaneous surface EMG of the bilateral orbicularis oculi, corrugator, nasalis, orbicularis oris, and masseter muscles, documenting whether typical movements occur during sleep.

A monitored therapeutic trial of botulinum toxin type A injected by a movement-disorders specialist into the clinically active facial muscles, beginning with the orbicularis oculi and adding perioral muscles if involved.
served: needle EMG of the affected muscles
